title: How an SSD remembers your files with no power
description: SSDs and phone storage trap electrons in tiny cells. Here's how that stores bits, and why cells wear out.

scenes.big: SSDs store data as trapped electrons
scenes.sub: no moving parts, no power needed
scenes.say: An SSD has no spinning parts and needs no power to remember your files. So what is it actually storing?

Each cell has a floating gate. Electrons get pushed in through a thin oxide layer and stay trapped. That charge is your data. Pack more charge levels into a cell and it holds more bits. That's cheaper and denser, but it endures fewer erases.
Every program and erase cycle wears a cell a little. Endurance is rated in those cycles, and the numbers shown are rough figures.
Unlike a hard drive's spinning platters, flash has no moving parts. A controller spreads writes around, called wear leveling, so no block dies first.

steps: Charge stays when power is off
Erasing pulls the charge back out
scenes.say: Saving a file pushes electrons into cells. They stay even without power. Erasing pulls them back out. Your phone's storage works on the same flash idea. Follow for more.
